newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese bank up for sale.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese bank up for sale.

text.p: Lebanon's central bank is seeking to sell Credit Libanais, a medium-size bank it acquired in 1989, and Beirut bankers say the sale could set off a long-awaited consolidation process in Lebanon's crowded banking system.
Nasser Saidi, Vice-Governor of the Bank of Lebanon, told Reuters the central bank was inviting bids for the sale of its 97 percent holding in CL in a private share placement.
Credit Libanais is a commercial and investment bank with an extensive credit card business whose 3.43 percent market share of deposits ranks 10th among Lebanon's 83 banks.
Its 45 branches comprise the biggest retail banking network in the country and include a Cyprus Offshore Banking Unit. It has one of the highest liquidity and capital adequacy ratios in the sector.
The Bank of Lebanon acquired CL as part payment of amounts owed to it after a famous financial crash in the 1980s involving al-Mashrek bank and the Intra group.

Said said bids are open until the end of June and that apart from existing legal and regulatory requirements no conditions had been set other than that the buyer should show liquid funds available to the tune of $100 million.
"In other words we want very serious bidders," Saidi said in an interview. "It would have to be somebody who had extremely solid financial footings."

CL's assets at end 1996 totalled $898 million -- 10th in the sector and 40 percent of top-ranked Banque de la Mediterranee Group. Shareholders' equity was eighth at $66 million and profits ranked 24th at $3.55 million.

Asked if the central bank had specified whether the buyer should be Lebanese or foreign, Saidi said: "We haven't placed any restrictions on that beyond current laws which provide that one-third of the shares of any Lebanese bank should be held by Lebanese nationals."
Indications of interest had been received from Arab countries as well as from Lebanese banks, he said.

The law allows the Bank of Lebanon to hold shares and securities in settlement of debts owed, but only for a limited period. Saidi said it had wanted to sell CL for some time and decided to go ahead after matters linked to Intra and al-Mashrek had been put in order.

"Putting the house in order has been done and has been done extremely well by Credit Libanais and its management...So we felt the time is appropriate for the central bank to remove itself as a major shareholder in it," he said.

Another factor in the timing was that Lebanon's banking sector has performed well for several years and there was substantial investor interest in the country, particularly in the financial and banking sector.
"The Banque du Liban also wanted to end a potential conflict of interest situation in which it was regulator and overseer of the banking system while owning a major bank," Saidi said.
"We felt that a private placement would be the best way to achieve that and would yield the best return on our investment, which is also an important consideration for us," he said.

Asked why the central bank did not sell CL shares on Beirut's re-emerging stock exchange, he said that since Lebanese banks were restricted to the sale of 30 percent of their shares on the stock market this would have left most CL shares in the hands of the central bank.

"We felt it would be better that whoever the ultimate purchaser is...if they wished to sell shares on the stock exchange or GDRs, would be best placed to do so rather than the central bank," Saidi said.
A senior Beirut banker who asked not to be identified welcomed the sale decision. He said CL was in good shape and but insisted it was very important that it remain in Lebanese hands.

"If a Lebanese bank buys it it will create awareness among other Lebanese banks of the need for consolidation, so this is a good opportunity to reach the level of consolidation we have been talking of for the last four years but have not achieved.
"If one of our rivals got it I would immediately look for something similar or be more open-minded about mergers or acquisitions," the banker said.

But asked whether the banking sector was excited by the sale, he said: "It's a complex deal because Credit Libanais owns a lot of fixed assets, including the Liberty Tower office block (in Beirut's Hamra district), and a credit card business.
"So it's not something crystal clear. It's worth studying it in depth," he said.
